title: Transactions: the money must not vanish rule (ACID)
story:
A transfer is two operations: take from one account, give to another. A machine can stop between them. If it does, the money is gone — subtracted from one place and never added to the other — and nothing in either operation was wrong.

That is the problem, and the shape of it is worth noticing before the solution. Neither step is incorrect. The fault is that a sequence of individually correct steps can be interrupted, and an interruption is not an error anyone wrote.

Jim Gray presented The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations at the seventh Very Large Data Bases conference in Cannes in September 1981, describing transactions in terms of atomicity — an all-or-nothing property — consistency, and durability, the survival of a committed transaction's effects after failures. His earlier Notes on Data Base Operating Systems of 1978 had already covered concurrency control, locking, recovery, logging, checkpointing and commit protocols, so the 1981 paper is a consolidation rather than an opening.

The analogy he used is the most useful thing in it. He compared the transaction concept to a legal contract, in which work can proceed provisionally before a commitment establishes the resulting state. That is exactly the right mental model: everything a transaction does is provisional until the commit, and the commit is the moment the provisional becomes binding.

Worth correcting one attribution, since it is nearly always given to Gray. The acronym is not his. It appears in Härder and Reuter's 1983 paper Principles of Transaction-Oriented Database Recovery in ACM Computing Surveys, which built on the earlier transaction processing work including Gray's, and which provides a terminological framework for describing recovery schemes conceptually rather than in an implementation-dependent way. Gray described the properties; Härder and Reuter named them. He received the 1998 Turing Award for seminal contributions to database and transaction processing research and technical leadership in system implementation.

Now the mechanism, which is more interesting than the acronym. The difficulty is that a crash can happen at any instant, including during the write that was supposed to make things safe — so there is no single write that can be relied upon to be atomic across a whole change.

The resolution is to stop trying to make the change atomic and make a record of the intention atomic instead. Before modifying anything, append a description of what is about to happen to a sequential log, and force it to durable storage. Only then perform the change. Now consider where a crash can land. Before the log record is durable: nothing happened, and nothing is expected to have happened. After the log record is durable but before the change is complete: the log says what was intended, so on restart the system reads it and finishes the work or undoes it. After both: nothing to do.

Every case is covered, and note what made that possible. The log is append-only and sequential, so a record is either wholly present or it is not — there is no state where half an intention exists. The hard problem was moved to a place where a single small durable write settles it.

The costs are real and are usually understated. That forcing of the log to durable storage sits on the critical path of every commit, which is why commit rate is bounded by storage latency rather than by processing speed, and why batching commits is such a common optimisation. The log also grows continuously and must be trimmed against checkpoints, which is a background process that can fall behind. And durability is only as good as the device's honesty — if hardware acknowledges a write it has merely buffered, the guarantee is void, and the database cannot detect this.

problem.name: Write the intention first
problem.shape: A change requires several steps and the machine can stop between any of them.
tell: a multi-step update has no transaction around it
recovery consists of inspecting data to guess what happened
a commit is acknowledged before anything reached durable storage
correctness arguments assume the process does not stop
problem.move: Make the record of the intention durable before performing the change, in a sequential append-only log forced to storage. Then every crash point is recoverable: either the intention is absent and nothing happened, or it is present and the work can be completed or undone.
problem.invariant: No single write can make a multi-step change atomic, but a small append is either wholly present or absent — so recording what is about to happen, durably, makes every interruption recoverable.
problem.breaks: Durability is only as strong as the storage device's honesty. If hardware acknowledges a write it has merely buffered, the guarantee is void and the database cannot detect it — so the property rests on a claim made by a component outside the system's control.

cost.time: forcing the log to durable storage is on the critical path of every commit, so commit rate is bounded by storage latency rather than processing speed
cost.space: the log grows continuously and must be trimmed against checkpoints, which is background work that can fall behind
cost.beats: writing the data directly and hoping, which is fast and loses money, and keeping everything in memory until done, which is fast and loses everything on a crash

worked.problem: What does the write-ahead log do, and how does it guarantee durability if the database crashes during a write?
worked.reasoning:
It makes the record of an intention durable before the intention is carried out, which converts an unbounded problem into one with a small number of recoverable cases.

The difficulty first, because the solution looks arbitrary without it. A crash can occur at any instant, including partway through the very write meant to make things safe. So there is no single write that can be relied on to make a whole change atomic — modifying several pages cannot be done in one indivisible step.

So stop trying to make the change atomic and make the record atomic instead. Before touching anything, append a description of what is about to happen to a sequential log and force it to durable storage. Then perform the change.

Now enumerate where a crash can land, which is what makes the argument convincing. Before the log record is durable: nothing happened and nothing is expected to have happened, so there is nothing to recover. After the log record is durable but before the change completes: the log states the intention, so on restart the system reads it and either completes the work or undoes it, depending on whether the transaction had committed. After both: nothing to do. Every case is covered.

The property that makes it work is worth naming, because it is where the atomicity actually comes from. The log is append-only and sequential, so a record is either wholly present or it is not — there is no state in which half an intention exists. The hard problem was relocated to a place where one small durable write settles it.

That is also the mental model Gray offered and it is a good one: a transaction is like a legal contract, in which work can proceed provisionally before a commitment establishes the resulting state. Everything is provisional until commit; commit is where provisional becomes binding.

The costs should be stated because they explain database behaviour that otherwise looks odd. The forced write to durable storage sits on the critical path of every commit, so commit rate is bounded by storage latency rather than processing speed — which is why batching commits is such a common optimisation, and why a system doing many small transactions is often slower than one doing few large ones. The log also grows continuously and has to be trimmed against checkpoints, a background process that can fall behind.

And the limitation I would want stated: durability is only as good as the device's honesty. If hardware acknowledges a write it has merely buffered in volatile memory, the guarantee is void, and the database has no way to detect that. The property rests on a claim made by a component outside its control, which is an uncomfortable place for the foundation of everything else to sit.

problem.practice: Find the setting in your database that controls whether commits force to durable storage, and the setting on your storage that controls write caching. If the second is lying, the first does nothing, and most people have never looked at either.

beats.broke: A transfer is two operations and a machine can stop between them, so an interruption leaves money subtracted from one place and never added to the other — with neither operation having been wrong.
beats.fix: Record the intention durably before performing it, in a sequential append-only log, so that after a crash the record says what was meant to happen and the work can be completed or undone.
beats.cost: The record must reach durable storage before a commit is acknowledged, which puts a physical write on the critical path of every transaction and bounds commit rate by storage latency.

interview.q: What does the write-ahead log do, and how does it guarantee durability if the database crashes during a write?
interview.trap: Explaining it as writing the data twice for safety. The point is not redundancy — it is that a small append is atomic where a multi-page change is not, so the intention can be made durable when the change cannot.

  MAKE THINGS SAFE. no single write is atomic across

     append the intention -> FORCE to durable storage
     -> then act

  a drive that acknowledges a buffered write VOIDS

takeaway: No single write can make a multi-step change atomic, so the fix is to make the record of the intention atomic instead — append it, force it to storage, then act, which leaves every crash point recoverable; and the acronym everyone attributes to Gray was actually coined by Härder and Reuter in 1983.
